component_claim: The test oracle problem: the hard part of testing is deciding correct vs. incorrect output, not generating inputs
title: The Oracle Problem in Software Testing: A Survey
org_author: Earl T. Barr, Mark Harman, Phil McMinn, Muzammil Shahbaz, Shin Yoo (UCL / Sheffield)
pub_date: 2015 (IEEE Transactions on Software Engineering, Vol. 41, No. 5)
source_type: Peer-reviewed survey, author's own institutional copy (primary)
quote_or_paraphrase: "Given an input for a system, the challenge of distinguishing the corresponding desired, correct behaviour from potentially incorrect behavior is called the 'test oracle problem.' ... Without test oracle automation, the human has to determine whether observed behaviour is correct."
caveats: Direct PDF fetch of the UCL mirror timed out in this session; the exact abstract text was retrieved via a web-search tool that quoted the paper's own abstract with a citation to this same URL, not independently re-rendered from the raw PDF in this pass. Used here to ground the report's core distinction: input/scenario generation and oracle computation are different problems with different automation risk profiles.

component_claim: Metamorphic testing as an oracle-substitute technique when a full formal oracle is impractical
title: A Survey on Metamorphic Testing
org_author: Sergio Segura, Gordon Fraser, Ana B. Sanchez, Antonio Ruiz-Cortes
pub_date: 2016 (IEEE Transactions on Software Engineering, Vol. 42, No. 9)
source_type: Peer-reviewed survey, institutional repository copy (primary)
quote_or_paraphrase: "A test oracle determines whether a test execution reveals a fault, often by comparing the observed program output to the expected output. This is not always practical... Metamorphic testing provides an alternative, where correctness is not determined by checking an individual concrete output, but by applying a transformation to a test input and observing how the program output 'morphs.'"
caveats: Confirms that even the academic alternatives to a full deterministic oracle (metamorphic relations) still require formally/programmatically defined, non-hallucinated relations between inputs and outputs - reinforcing rather than weakening the case for a scripted oracle over an LLM-generated one for a case with a well-defined v1/v2 mapping.

component_claim: LLMs applied to test oracle automation carry named, unresolved risks (oracle deficiencies, data leakage) even in dedicated LLM-oracle research
title: Test Oracle Automation in the era of LLMs
source_type: Position/discussion paper, arXiv (primary, verified via arXiv API)
quote_or_paraphrase: "This paper aims to enable discussions on the potential of using LLMs for test oracle automation, along with the challenges that may emerge... to initiate discussions on the primary threats that SE researchers must consider when employing LLMs for oracle automation, encompassing concerns regarding oracle deficiencies and data leakages."
caveats: Abstract retrieved directly from the arXiv API (export.arxiv.org), not a secondary summary. This is a paper written specifically to explore LLM-generated oracles favorably, yet its own framing names 'oracle deficiencies' and 'data leakages' as primary threats requiring discussion - i.e., even proponents flag this as unresolved, not a solved problem.

component_claim: Empirical evidence that LLM-generated oracles have measured strengths/limitations that vary by prompting and context, not a settled reliable capability
title: Understanding LLM-Driven Test Oracle Generation
source_type: Empirical study, arXiv (primary, verified via arXiv API)
quote_or_paraphrase: "Existing techniques primarily generate regression oracles that predicate on the implemented behavior of the class under test. They do not address the oracle problem... We investigate how different prompting strategies and levels of contextual input impact the quality of LLM-generated oracles. Our findings offer insights into the strengths and limitations of LLM-based oracle generation."
caveats: Abstract retrieved directly from the arXiv API. Explicitly distinguishes regression-style (implementation-derived, not correctness-derived) oracles from oracles that reflect intended/specified behavior - the same distinction this report relies on to keep the migration oracle scripted from the v1/v2 mapping rules rather than LLM-inferred.

component_claim: Property-based testing: generate many inputs automatically and check declared properties, rather than hand-writing example-based expected outputs
title: QuickCheck: A Lightweight Tool for Random Testing of Haskell Programs
source_type: Peer-reviewed conference paper, ACM Digital Library (primary; abstract text via secondary academic mirror)
quote_or_paraphrase: "QuickCheck is a tool that helps Haskell programmers formulate and test properties of their programs. Properties are expressed as Haskell functions, which QuickCheck automatically tests using randomly generated input data."
caveats: ACM's own page (fetched directly) confirms publication metadata (title, venue, 2000-09-01 date) but its abstract text is paywalled; the quoted text was obtained via a secondary academic-mirror summary (pls-lab.org / academia.edu), not independently re-derived from ACM's full text in this pass. Cited as the origin of property-based testing generally, which JSON-Schema-driven generators (row below) descend from; QuickCheck itself checks properties, it does not compute or replace a deterministic expected-output oracle.

component_claim: Deriving a property-based test data generator directly from a JSON Schema document
title: hypothesis-jsonschema (README)
source_type: Open-source project documentation (primary)
quote_or_paraphrase: "A Hypothesis strategy for generating data that matches some JSON schema... The public API consists of just one function: hypothesis_jsonschema.from_schema, which takes a JSON schema and returns a strategy for allowed JSON objects."
caveats: Directly demonstrates the deterministic, tool-based path already available for turning a v1/v2 JSON Schema into generated example instances, with no LLM involved; supports the report's position that schema-conformant instance generation is a solved, scriptable problem and JSON Schema drafts 04/05/07 are supported (07 covers most migration-schema needs).

component_claim: Deterministic, seeded generation of schema-conformant fake JSON instances
title: json-schema-faker (README)
source_type: Open-source project documentation (primary)
quote_or_paraphrase: "Generate valid JSON data from JSON Schema definitions. Zero production dependencies.... Deterministic output via seeded PRNG (Mulberry32)... Composition keywords: allOf, anyOf, oneOf, not, if/then/else... $ref resolution with cycle detection."
caveats: A second, independently maintained tool confirming the same point as hypothesis-jsonschema: syntactically-valid, schema-conformant instance generation (including schema composition and $ref) is an existing, deterministic, script-level capability, not something that requires an LLM to produce merely-valid instances.

component_claim: JSON Schema natively supports embedding illustrative example values in a schema via a non-validating annotation keyword
title: Annotations - Understanding JSON Schema
source_type: Open specification reference documentation (primary)
quote_or_paraphrase: "The examples keyword is a place to provide an array of examples that validate against the schema. This isn't used for validation, but may help with explaining the effect and purpose of the schema to a reader."
caveats: Confirms that authoring illustrative examples against a schema is a native, well-defined JSON Schema concept; relevant background for scenario-metadata design but not itself a generation or fuzzing tool, and the keyword is explicitly non-validating (examples are not guaranteed to conform).

component_claim: Combinatorial (t-way) testing / covering arrays: most faults are triggered by interactions of a small number of parameters, so systematically covering low-order interactions is an efficient, deterministic alternative to exhaustive input enumeration
title: Practical Combinatorial Testing (NIST SP 800-142)
org_author: D. Richard Kuhn, Raghu N. Kacker, Yu Lei (NIST)
source_type: Government/standards-body technical publication (primary)
quote_or_paraphrase: "The key insight underlying t-way combinatorial testing is that not every parameter contributes to every fault and most faults are caused by interactions between a relatively small number of parameters... discusses advanced topics such as the use of formal models of software to determine the expected results for each set of test inputs."
caveats: Directly supports using covering arrays over the v1/v2 field/rule interaction space to bound corpus size while preserving coverage of cross-field interactions - and NIST's own framing keeps expected-result determination as a separate, formal-model-based step from input generation, matching this report's oracle/generator split.

component_claim: Microsoft PICT: a first-party, deterministic pairwise/combinatorial test-case generator used to produce compact parameter-interaction test suites from a declared parameter model
title: microsoft/pict (README)
source_type: Vendor open-source project documentation (primary)
quote_or_paraphrase: "PICT generates test cases and test configurations... Prepare a model file detailing the parameters of the interface... PICT generates a compact set of parameter value choices that represent the test cases you should use to get comprehensive combinatorial coverage of your parameters... testing all pairs is an effective alternative to exhaustive testing."
caveats: First-party Microsoft tooling for exactly the combinatorial/covering-array technique in the row above; directly usable, deterministic, and open-source - a concrete off-the-shelf option for generating the parameter-combination skeleton of the corpus from a declared model of v1/v2 fields, distinct from any AI-authored scenario semantics layered on top.

component_claim: Grammar-based generation produces syntactically valid inputs by construction, which is markedly more effective than unstructured random fuzzing for structured formats
title: Efficient Grammar Fuzzing - The Fuzzing Book
org_author: Andreas Zeller et al. (CISPA / Saarland University)
source_type: Academic online textbook (primary)
quote_or_paraphrase: "In the chapter on grammars, we have seen how to use grammars for very effective and efficient testing. In this chapter, we refine the previous string-based algorithm into a tree-based algorithm, which is much faster and allows for much more control over the production of fuzz inputs."
caveats: A JSON Schema is itself a grammar-like structural constraint; this establishes the general, deterministic technique (structure-aware generation beats blind random fuzzing for validity) that JSON-Schema-driven generators such as json-schema-faker and hypothesis-jsonschema (rows above) already implement for this exact problem shape.

component_claim: Grammar/structure-aware fuzzing found hundreds of real bugs in production C compilers by generating large volumes of syntactically valid, semantically constrained random programs - establishing the technique's real-world effectiveness, independent of any LLM
title: Finding and Understanding Bugs in C Compilers
org_author: Xuejun Yang, Yang Chen, Eric Eide, John Regehr (University of Utah)
source_type: Peer-reviewed conference paper, ACM Digital Library (primary; abstract text via secondary academic mirror)
quote_or_paraphrase: "We created Csmith, a randomized test-case generation tool, and spent three years using it to find compiler bugs... more than 325 previously unknown bugs... Csmith generates programs that cover a large subset of C while avoiding the undefined and unspecified behaviors that would destroy its ability to automatically find wrong-code bugs."
caveats: ACM's own page confirms venue/date/authors but the abstract text was retrieved via a secondary mirror (flux.utah.edu / academia.edu), not independently re-derived from ACM's paywalled full text in this pass. Cited as the strongest evidence that deterministic, constraint-aware generative fuzzing (no LLM) scales to finding real, previously-unknown defects; directly analogous to generating diverse deterministic v1/v2 fixtures.

component_claim: Mutation testing: deliberately seeding small, systematic faults ('mutants') into a program under test, and using whether a test suite detects (kills) them as a measure of the suite's fault-detection effectiveness
title: Hints on Test Data Selection: Help for the Practicing Programmer
org_author: Richard A. DeMillo, Richard J. Lipton, Frederick G. Sayward
source_type: Foundational peer-reviewed paper (bibliographic record verified directly; original text paywalled)
quote_or_paraphrase: Introduced the coupling effect hypothesis and the technique of judging test data adequacy by whether it can distinguish a program from systematically mutated versions of itself - the origin of mutation testing as a test-suite-effectiveness measure.
caveats: This session verified the paper's existence, authors, venue, and 1978 date directly via the CERIAS Purdue bibliographic record, but the original IEEE Computer text is paywalled and was not independently fetched; the coupling-effect description is a well-established paraphrase corroborated by multiple independent bibliographic/secondary sources (dblp, SciSpace, researchr), not a verbatim quote from the primary text.

component_claim: Mutation testing has matured over three decades into a set of established, practical tools and techniques for measuring test-suite fault-detection effectiveness
title: An Analysis and Survey of the Development of Mutation Testing
pub_date: 2011 (IEEE Transactions on Software Engineering, Vol. 37, No. 5)
source_type: Peer-reviewed survey, author's own institutional repository copy (primary)
quote_or_paraphrase: "Mutation Testing is a fault-based software testing technique that has been widely studied for over three decades... These analyses provide evidence that Mutation Testing techniques and tools are reaching a state of maturity and applicability."
caveats: The PDF was fetched directly from UCL's CREST repository in this session, confirming it is the correct file, but the extracted content was raw/garbled PDF byte-stream rather than cleanly rendered text; the quoted abstract text matches what a web-search tool independently reported as the paper's own abstract with a citation to this same URL.

component_claim: 'Mutation score' / mutant kill rate is the standard, tool-computed metric for how effectively a test suite (or, by direct analogy, a test corpus) detects seeded faults - directly usable as the 'hidden mutant kill rate' metric for corpus effectiveness
title: Basic Concepts - Pitest (PIT)
source_type: Open-source project documentation (primary)
quote_or_paraphrase: "By applying the mutation operators PIT will generate a number... of mutants. These are Java classes which contain a mutation... which should make them behave differently from the unmutated class. PIT will then run your tests using this mutant instead of the unmutated class. An effective set of tests should fail in the presence of the mutant."
caveats: Directly operational definition of 'killed' vs. 'survived' vs. 'no coverage' mutants that this report's hidden-mutant-kill-rate metric is modeled on; PIT itself targets Java bytecode, so an equivalent mutation layer for the migration script/oracle (or a purpose-built mutant generator for the mapping-rule implementation) would need to be built for this project's language, but the metric definition and operator taxonomy transfer directly.

component_claim: Search-based software test data generation (metaheuristic/evolutionary search over the input space, guided by a fitness function) is an established deterministic-algorithm technique distinct from both example-based and AI/LLM-based generation
title: Search-Based Software Test Data Generation: A Survey
pub_date: 2004 (Software Testing, Verification and Reliability, Vol. 14, No. 2)
source_type: Peer-reviewed survey, author's own institutional copy (primary)
quote_or_paraphrase: Test data generation is formulated as a search/optimization problem: test goals are mapped to fitness functions and a search algorithm (e.g., evolutionary algorithm, simulated annealing) is used to find inputs that satisfy structural or functional test criteria, including through long dependency chains (the 'chaining problem').
caveats: The PDF was fetched directly from the author's own site in this session, confirming the correct file, but the extracted content was raw/garbled PDF byte-stream rather than cleanly rendered text in this pass; the paraphrase reflects a well-established, widely-cited characterization of this survey's contribution rather than a verbatim quote independently re-derived here.

component_claim: EvoSuite: a mature, deterministic-algorithm (evolutionary search) tool that automatically generates test suites (including assertions) to maximize code coverage, without an LLM
title: EvoSuite - Automatic Test Suite Generation for Java
source_type: Open-source project site (primary)
quote_or_paraphrase: EvoSuite uses evolutionary search to generate JUnit test suites targeting coverage criteria (e.g., branch coverage), producing assertions that capture current program behavior, and is documented across multiple peer-reviewed publications (ESEC/FSE 2011, ACM TOSEM 2014).
caveats: Cited to establish that mature, deterministic search-based test generation tooling for structural coverage already exists as prior art; this report treats EvoSuite-style structural search as a candidate deterministic technique for input generation, not as a substitute for a semantics-aware scenario-design step or for oracle computation, since EvoSuite's generated assertions encode observed behavior, not a specification-derived correct answer.

component_claim: Combining deterministic search-based test generation with an LLM specifically to escape coverage plateaus is a documented, evaluated hybrid pattern - LLM proposes candidate inputs, a deterministic search process still drives and validates exploration
title: CodaMosa: Escaping Coverage Plateaus in Test Generation with Pre-trained Large Language Models
org_author: Caroline Lemieux, Jeevana Priya Inala, Shuvendu K. Lahiri, Siddhartha Sen (Microsoft Research / UC Berkeley)
source_type: Peer-reviewed conference paper, publisher's own research page (primary)
quote_or_paraphrase: "CODAMOSA conducts SBST until its coverage improvements stall, then asks Codex to provide example test cases for under-covered functions. These examples help SBST redirect its search to more useful areas of the search space. On an evaluation over 486 benchmarks, CODAMOSA achieves statistically significantly higher coverage on many more benchmarks... than it reduces coverage on... compared to SBST and LLM-only baselines."
caveats: Directly supports this report's hybrid-arm design: an LLM's role is best evidenced as suggesting candidate inputs/scenarios to unstick a deterministic process, not as replacing the deterministic search/generation or, by extension, the oracle; note CodaMosa targets code coverage of the implementation under test, a different coverage notion than this report's semantic/path coverage of migration mapping rules.

component_claim: Empirical, large-scale evidence on LLM-generated test quality: LLM-only test generation can reach useful coverage but must be measured against redundancy/diversity (originality vs. existing tests) as an explicit metric, not assumed
title: An Empirical Evaluation of Using Large Language Models for Automated Unit Test Generation
org_author: Max Schafer, Sarah Nadi, Aryaz Eghbali, Frank Tip
source_type: Peer-reviewed empirical study, arXiv (primary, verified via arXiv API)
quote_or_paraphrase: "The generated tests achieve a median statement coverage of 70.2% and branch coverage of 52.8%... We also find that 92.8% of TestPilot's generated tests have no more than 50% similarity with existing tests (as measured by normalized edit distance), with none of them being exact copies... the effectiveness of the approach is influenced by the size and training set of the LLM, but does not fundamentally depend on the specific model."
caveats: Abstract retrieved directly from the arXiv API. Directly usable as the source of this report's 'redundancy/diversity' metric definition (normalized edit distance against a reference set, percentage of near-duplicates) for scoring AI-proposed corpus items; also evidence that LLM test-generation quality is model-size-sensitive, relevant to the parent-only vs. delegated-cheap-model evaluation arms.

component_claim: Differential testing (running two or more comparable implementations/versions on the same generated inputs and flagging divergent outputs) is an established, deterministic technique directly analogous to comparing a v1 and v2 system's behavior on a shared corpus
title: Differential Testing for Software
org_author: William M. McKeeman (Digital Equipment Corporation / Compaq)
source_type: Industry technical journal paper, institutional mirror (primary; abstract via secondary summary)
quote_or_paraphrase: "Differential testing... requires that two or more comparable systems be available to the tester. These systems are presented with an exhaustive series of mechanically generated test cases. If (or when) the results differ or one of the systems loops indefinitely or crashes, the tester has a candidate for a bug-exposing test."
caveats: Abstract text obtained via a web-search tool summary rather than independently re-fetched from the Tufts mirror in this pass. Directly analogous to, but not identical with, this report's migration scenario: a deterministic v1-to-v2 mapping-rule oracle is closer to a specification-derived oracle than to comparing two independently-evolved implementations, but the mechanically-generated, exhaustive-series framing is the same generator/oracle split this report recommends.

component_claim: GitHub Copilot documents a subagent mechanism where a specialized custom agent runs isolated work and the parent orchestrates/receives results, matching this repository's own reference platform for the delegation half of any Agent Skill Pattern reference
title: Custom agents and sub-agent orchestration
source_type: Vendor product documentation (primary)
quote_or_paraphrase: "Custom agents are lightweight agent definitions you attach to a session. Each agent has its own system prompt, tool restrictions, and optional MCP servers. When a user's request matches an agent's expertise, the Copilot runtime automatically delegates to that agent as a sub-agent - running it in an isolated context."
caveats: Re-verified directly in this session (not merely re-cited from the repository's existing prior-art.md) to independently ground this report's reference-contract recommendation on the same platform documentation already used elsewhere in this repository; describes the general subagent mechanism, not anything specific to test-corpus generation.

component_claim: GitHub Copilot documents Agent Skills as a discovery/routing mechanism loaded only when relevant, the same progressive-disclosure precedent this repository's pattern already relies on for any new reference, including one for corpus design
title: About agent skills
source_type: Vendor product documentation (primary)
quote_or_paraphrase: "Agent skills are folders of instructions, scripts, and resources that Copilot can load when relevant to improve its performance in specialized tasks. The Agent Skills specification is an open standard, used by a range of different AI systems."
caveats: Re-verified directly in this session. Confirms the routing/discovery mechanism a corpus-design Skill in this pattern would use is the same general-purpose mechanism already documented and already used by this repository's existing ascii-art reference implementation - not a corpus-generation-specific feature.
